chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ashyam, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I heard him saying: 'The time for al-Maghrib is when the redness disappears from the east.'

'And do you know how that is?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Because the east overlooks upon the west like this,' and he raised his right hand above his left, 'So when it disappears from over here, the redness goes away from over there.'

key_terms.الحُمرة: Redness/reddish glow — the evening twilight that persists in the east after sunset, used here as the marker for Maghrib time
key_terms.المشرق: The east/eastern horizon — where the redness must disappear before Maghrib time begins
key_terms.مُطِلّ: Overlooking, elevated over — the east is geographically/cosmologically elevated relative to the west, allowing it to reflect light longer
key_terms.وقت المغرب: The time (waqt) of al-Maghrib prayer — a major jurisprudential question in Islamic fiqh

ai.seo_question: When does the time for Maghrib prayer begin according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) defines the onset time of the Maghrib prayer as when the redness (the post-sunset twilight glow) vanishes from the eastern horizon. He illustrates this with a physical demonstration — raising his right hand above his left — to explain that the eastern sky, being elevated, reflects sunlight even after the sun has set in the west, and only when the sun descends far enough below the western horizon does that reflected glow in the east disappear, marking the true beginning of Maghrib. This hadith was significant in the Shia jurisprudential tradition, countering those who held that Maghrib begins immediately at sunset regardless of twilight.
